subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: The diagram shows the path of a ball launched over level ground; air resistance is negligible. What is the direction of the ball's momentum at point P?
options: Down and to the right, along the path at point P
Straight down, the direction of the gravitational force
Up and to the right, parallel to the launch velocity
Up and to the right, from the launch point to P
optionWhy: Momentum, p⃗ = mv⃗, has the direction of the velocity. The velocity is tangent to the path in the direction of travel, and at P, past the highest point, the ball is moving down and to the right.

A student who thinks an object's momentum points along the net force on it picks this. The gravitational force points down and changes the vertical velocity, but the momentum points along the velocity, which at P is down and to the right.

A student who thinks a launched ball keeps the motion it was given picks this. Once launched, the vertical velocity component changes while the horizontal one stays constant, so the direction of motion turns along the path.

A student who takes the direction of velocity to be the direction of the displacement from the start picks this. That line gives where the ball is relative to the launch point, not the direction in which it is moving at P.
questions.explain: Momentum, p⃗ = mv⃗, has the direction of the velocity. The velocity is tangent to the path in the direction of travel, and at P, past the highest point, the ball is moving down and to the right.
questions.working: Momentum has the direction of the velocity, which is tangent to the path in the direction of travel. At P the ball is past the highest point and moving down and to the right.

questions.q: Two cars collide at an intersection and both are badly dented. To find the cars' velocities just after the collision, a student models each car as an object, a single point with the car's mass. Which claim about the student's choice is correct?
options: It is valid, since only the cars' states just before and just after the collision are used.
It is not valid, since each car's shape changes while the two cars are in contact with each other.
It is not valid, since each car is large compared with how far it moves during the collision.
It is valid, since each car's mass really is concentrated at its center of mass.
optionWhy: A collision analysis compares the states just before and just after the collision, and each car's state is described by its mass and velocity. How the cars deform during the collision does not enter, so each can be modeled as an object.

A student who thinks a body that deforms cannot be modeled as an object picks this. The deformation happens during the collision, but the analysis uses only the states just before and just after it, so the deformation need not be described.
A student who thinks only tiny bodies can be modeled as objects picks this. Whether the object model applies depends on whether a body's internal structure matters to the analysis, not on its size.

A student who takes the object model literally picks this. A car's mass is spread through the car; the object model is a modeling choice that is justified here because only the states just before and just after the collision are analyzed.
questions.explain: A collision analysis compares the states just before and just after the collision, and each car's state is described by its mass and velocity. How the cars deform during the collision does not enter, so each can be modeled as an object.

questions.q: An object of mass m moves along the x-axis. Its position is given by x(t) = Ct² − Dt³, where C and D are positive constants and t is time. Which expression gives the object's momentum at time t?
options: p = m(Ct² − Dt³)
p = 2m(C − 3Dt)
p = mt(C − Dt)
p = m(2Ct − 3Dt²)
optionWhy: A student who takes the velocity from the position itself, rather than from its rate of change, picks this: it is m times x(t). Velocity is dx/dt, the slope of the position–time graph, not its height.
A student who computes momentum as mass times acceleration picks this: d²x/dt² = 2C − 6Dt, and m(2C − 6Dt) = 2m(C − 3Dt). That product is the net force; momentum is mass times velocity, dx/dt.
A student who divides the position by the time picks this: x/t = Ct − Dt², and m(x/t) = mt(C − Dt). That is an average velocity since t = 0, not the velocity at time t, which is dx/dt = 2Ct − 3Dt².
Momentum is mass times velocity, and the velocity is the derivative of position: v = dx/dt = 2Ct − 3Dt². So p = m(2Ct − 3Dt²).
questions.explain: Momentum is mass times velocity, and the velocity is the derivative of position: v = dx/dt = 2Ct − 3Dt². So p = m(2Ct − 3Dt²).
questions.working: v = dx/dt = 2Ct − 3Dt², so p = mv = m(2Ct − 3Dt²). Checks of the distractors: mx = m(Ct² − Dt³); m(x/t) = mt(C − Dt); m(dv/dt) = m(2C − 6Dt) = 2m(C − 3Dt).

questions.q: A 2.4 kg ball moves in the xy-plane with a speed of 2.5 m/s, in a direction 37° above the +x-axis. What is the y-component of the ball's momentum? (sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80.)
options: 4.8 kg·m/s
6.0 kg·m/s
3.6 kg·m/s
7.5 kg·m/s
optionWhy: A student who uses the cosine for the y-component picks this: (2.4)(2.5)(0.80) = 4.8. The angle is measured from the x-axis, so the y-component is the side opposite it, mv sin 37°.
A student who takes a component to be the whole magnitude picks this: mv = (2.4)(2.5) = 6.0. The momentum points at 37° to the x-axis, so its y-component is only the part mv sin 37°.
The momentum points along the velocity, so its y-component is m times the velocity's y-component: p_y = mv sin 37° = (2.4 kg)(2.5 m/s)(0.60) = 3.6 kg·m/s.
A student who calculates kinetic energy in place of momentum picks this: (1/2)(2.4)(2.5)² = 7.5, which is in joules, not kg·m/s. Momentum is mv, and its y-component is mv sin 37°.
questions.explain: The momentum points along the velocity, so its y-component is m times the velocity's y-component: p_y = mv sin 37° = (2.4 kg)(2.5 m/s)(0.60) = 3.6 kg·m/s.
questions.working: Momentum has the direction of the velocity, so p_y = mv_y = mv sin 37° = (2.4 kg)(2.5 m/s)(0.60) = 3.6 kg·m/s.

questions.q: Cart 1 and cart 2 have equal kinetic energies. The mass of cart 1 is four times the mass of cart 2. What is the ratio p₁/p₂ of the magnitudes of their momenta?
optionWhy: Writing K = p²/(2m) gives p = √(2mK). With equal kinetic energies, p₁/p₂ = √(m₁/m₂) = √4 = 2.00. Equivalently, cart 1 moves at half the speed of cart 2, and 4 × 1/2 = 2.

A student who treats momentum and kinetic energy as the same quantity picks this: equal kinetic energies would mean equal momenta. Since K = p²/(2m), equal K gives p proportional to √m, so the heavier cart has the larger momentum.

A student who judges momentum by mass alone picks this: four times the mass, four times the momentum. With equal kinetic energies the heavier cart moves more slowly, at half the speed, so its momentum is only twice as large.
A student who judges momentum by speed alone picks this: cart 1 moves at half the speed of cart 2. Momentum is mv, and cart 1's four-times-larger mass more than makes up for its lower speed.
questions.explain: Writing K = p²/(2m) gives p = √(2mK). With equal kinetic energies, p₁/p₂ = √(m₁/m₂) = √4 = 2.00. Equivalently, cart 1 moves at half the speed of cart 2, and 4 × 1/2 = 2.
questions.working: K = (1/2)mv² = p²/(2m), so p = √(2mK). With equal K, p₁/p₂ = √(m₁/m₂) = √4 = 2.00. (Equivalently, v₁/v₂ = √(m₂/m₁) = 1/2, and p₁/p₂ = 4 × 1/2 = 2.)

questions.q: A clay ball and a rubber ball have equal masses. Each is thrown horizontally at a wall with the same speed. The clay ball sticks to the wall; the rubber ball rebounds with the same speed it had before the collision. How does the magnitude of the impulse delivered by the wall to the rubber ball compare with that delivered to the clay ball?
options: The clay ball's is larger, since the wall must absorb all its motion.
The rubber ball's is twice as large, since its momentum reverses.
They are equal, since both balls reach the wall with equal momenta.
The rubber ball's is zero, since its speed after the collision is unchanged.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the object stopped dead receives the larger impulse picks this. The wall must stop both balls; for the rubber ball it must also send it back at the same speed, so the rubber ball's change in momentum is larger.

Taking the initial direction as positive, the clay ball's change in momentum is 0 − mv = −mv, and the rubber ball's is (−mv) − mv = −2mv. The impulse equals the change in momentum, so the rubber ball's is twice as large.
A student who thinks the wall only stops each ball picks this. Equal initial momenta do not give equal changes; the wall also pushes the rubber ball back out, which doubles its change in momentum.
A student who takes the change in momentum to be the change in its size picks this. The speed is unchanged but the direction reverses, so the change in momentum, and the impulse, has magnitude 2mv.
questions.explain: Taking the initial direction as positive, the clay ball's change in momentum is 0 − mv = −mv, and the rubber ball's is (−mv) − mv = −2mv. The impulse equals the change in momentum, so the rubber ball's is twice as large.

questions.q: An egg dropped onto a pillow does not break, but an identical egg dropped from the same height onto a hard floor does break. In both cases the egg comes to rest. Which reasoning best explains the difference?
options: The pillow is soft and gives way, so the egg's change in momentum on the pillow is smaller than on the floor.
The hard floor pushes up on the egg, but the soft pillow only absorbs the egg's motion without pushing.
The pillow acts on the egg for a longer time, so the egg's change in momentum is larger but gentler.
The egg's momentum change is the same on both, but the pillow takes longer, so the average force is smaller.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a soft landing reduces the change in momentum picks this. Both eggs go from the same momentum to rest, so the change is the same; the pillow changes only how long it takes.
A student who thinks surfaces such as pillows are passive picks this. The pillow does push up on the egg; that push is what stops it, with a smaller force acting for a longer time.

A student who thinks a longer contact time means a larger effect picks this. The egg's change in momentum is fixed by its initial and final states and is the same on both; a longer time means a smaller average force.

Both eggs arrive with the same momentum and end at rest, so their changes in momentum, and the impulses of the net forces on them, are equal. The pillow spreads that change over a longer time, so the average net force on the egg, Δp/Δt, is smaller.
questions.explain: Both eggs arrive with the same momentum and end at rest, so their changes in momentum, and the impulses of the net forces on them, are equal. The pillow spreads that change over a longer time, so the average net force on the egg, Δp/Δt, is smaller.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how Newton's second law in the form F_net = ma is related to the relationship F_net = dp/dt?
options: F_net = ma and F_net = dp/dt are equivalent for every system, since p = mv.
F_net = dp/dt applies during collisions, and F_net = ma applies at other times.
F_net = dp/dt gives the average force over an interval; F_net = ma, the force at an instant.
F_net = ma is what F_net = dp/dt becomes when the system's mass is constant.
optionWhy: A student who thinks F_net = ma holds for every system picks this. If the mass changes, dp/dt is not m dv/dt: a conveyor belt moving at constant velocity while sand lands on it needs a net force although a = 0.
A student who treats momentum relationships as rules only for collisions picks this. F_net = dp/dt applies to any system at any time; F_net = ma is its form for constant mass.

A student who reads dp/dt as Δp/Δt, an average over an interval, picks this. dp/dt is the instantaneous rate of change of momentum, so F_net = dp/dt gives the net force at each instant; for constant mass it equals ma at that same instant.
With p = mv and m constant, dp/dt = m dv/dt = ma, so F_net = dp/dt reduces to F_net = ma. When the mass changes, dp/dt includes the change in mass and the two are not equivalent.
questions.explain: With p = mv and m constant, dp/dt = m dv/dt = ma, so F_net = dp/dt reduces to F_net = ma. When the mass changes, dp/dt includes the change in mass and the two are not equivalent.

questions.q: A hand pulls block A to the right across a rough horizontal surface, and a light horizontal string joins A to block B. The diagram shows the horizontal forces exerted on each block; the vertical forces on each block are balanced. What is the magnitude of the rate of change of the momentum of the two-block system?
optionWhy: A student who takes the pulled block as the system picks this: the net force on A alone is 30 − 15 − 5.0 = 10 N. That is the rate of change of A's momentum; the two-block system also includes B, and the string's pulls cancel within it.

A student who takes the net force to be the applied pull picks this. The two friction forces are also external forces on the system and act opposite to the pull, so they reduce the net external force to 20 N.

For the two-block system the string's pulls on A and on B are internal and cancel. The external horizontal forces are the 30 N pull and the two 5.0 N friction forces, so dp/dt = F_net,ext = 30 N − 5.0 N − 5.0 N = 20 N.

A student who adds the sizes of all the forces in the diagram picks this: 30 + 15 + 15 + 5.0 + 5.0 = 70. Forces add as vectors: the friction forces point opposite to the pull, and the two tensions are internal and cancel.
questions.explain: For the two-block system the string's pulls on A and on B are internal and cancel. The external horizontal forces are the 30 N pull and the two 5.0 N friction forces, so dp/dt = F_net,ext = 30 N − 5.0 N − 5.0 N = 20 N.
questions.working: System: both blocks. The string tensions, 15 N on each block in opposite directions, are internal and cancel. External horizontal forces: 30 N to the right; friction 5.0 N + 5.0 N to the left. dp/dt = F_net,ext = 30 − 5.0 − 5.0 = 20 N, to the right.

questions.q: The net force on an object moving along the x-axis is F(t) = 3.0 + 6.0t², where F is in newtons and t is in seconds. What is the impulse delivered to the object from t = 0 to t = 2.0 s?
options: 22 N·s
54 N·s
30 N·s
24 N·s
optionWhy: The impulse is the integral of the net force over the interval: J = ∫₀²(3.0 + 6.0t²) dt = [3.0t + 2.0t³] from 0 to 2.0 s = 6.0 + 16 = 22 N·s.
A student who treats the force as constant at its final value picks this: F(2.0 s) = 27 N, and 27 N × 2.0 s = 54 N·s. The force was smaller earlier in the interval, so the impulse is less.
A student who averages the force's end values picks this: (3.0 N + 27 N)/2 = 15 N, and 15 N × 2.0 s = 30 N·s. The force grows as t², not linearly, so its time average is 11 N, not 15 N.
A student who uses the force's rate of change picks this: dF/dt = 12t, which is 24 at t = 2.0 s. That is a slope, in N/s; impulse is the area under the force–time graph, ∫F dt.
questions.explain: The impulse is the integral of the net force over the interval: J = ∫₀²(3.0 + 6.0t²) dt = [3.0t + 2.0t³] from 0 to 2.0 s = 6.0 + 16 = 22 N·s.

questions.q: Three carts of different masses move along a straight, level track with different velocities. A student wants to analyze the three carts as a single system. Which statement about the velocity of this system is correct?
options: It cannot have a single velocity unless the three carts all move with the same velocity.
Its velocity is the average of the three carts' velocities, with each cart counted equally.
Its velocity is that of its most massive cart, whose motion dominates the motion of the system.
It has one velocity, its center-of-mass velocity, though the carts' velocities differ.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a group of objects has a velocity only when it moves as one piece picks this. The center-of-mass velocity is defined for any system, however its parts move.

A student who takes a plain average of the velocities picks this. The system's velocity is the mass-weighted average, (Σ m_i v⃗_i)/(Σ m_i); a plain average gives it only if the carts have equal masses, and these carts do not.
A student who identifies the system with its most massive part picks this. Every cart contributes to v⃗_cm in proportion to its mass, so in general v⃗_cm differs from the velocity of any one cart.

Any collection of objects can be described as one system with one center-of-mass velocity, v⃗_cm = (Σ m_i v⃗_i)/(Σ m_i). It exists whatever the carts' individual velocities, and the system's total momentum is (Σ m_i)v⃗_cm.
questions.explain: Any collection of objects can be described as one system with one center-of-mass velocity, v⃗_cm = (Σ m_i v⃗_i)/(Σ m_i). It exists whatever the carts' individual velocities, and the system's total momentum is (Σ m_i)v⃗_cm.

questions.q: A cart moves at constant velocity along a level track with negligible friction. A spring inside the cart then launches a small block forward, and the block slides ahead of the cart along the same track. How does the velocity of the center of mass of the cart–block system after the launch compare with its velocity before the launch?
options: It is greater, since the spring gives the block extra forward momentum during the launch.
It is unchanged, since the spring's forces on the cart and the block are internal.
It is smaller, since the cart, which is the most massive part, slows down in the launch.
It is not defined, since the cart and block now move with different velocities.
optionWhy: A student who thinks an internal push adds momentum to the system picks this. The spring gives the block forward momentum but gives the cart an equal amount of backward momentum, so the total is unchanged.

The spring pushes the block forward and the cart backward with equal and opposite forces, which are internal to the cart–block system. With no net external force, the system's total momentum, and so v⃗_cm, is unchanged.

A student who takes the system's velocity to be that of its most massive part picks this. The cart does slow down, but the block speeds up by an equal and opposite momentum change, so v⃗_cm is unchanged.

A student who thinks a system has a velocity only when its parts move together picks this. v⃗_cm = (Σ m_i v⃗_i)/(Σ m_i) is defined for any system; here it equals the velocity the cart had before the launch.
questions.explain: The spring pushes the block forward and the cart backward with equal and opposite forces, which are internal to the cart–block system. With no net external force, the system's total momentum, and so v⃗_cm, is unchanged.

questions.q: A ball is released from rest and falls toward the ground. Air resistance is negligible. While the ball falls, which system has a total momentum that stays constant?
options: The ball alone, since no other object collides with the ball while it is falling.
No system, since the gravitational force on the ball is an external force on any system.
The ball–Earth system, since the gravitational forces in it are internal.
The Earth alone, since its very large mass keeps its momentum from changing.
optionWhy: A student who links changes in momentum only to collisions picks this. The gravitational force is a net external force on the ball alone, so its momentum increases downward at the rate mg.

A student who treats gravity as external in every case picks this. Whether a force is internal or external depends on the system chosen: with the Earth included, the gravitational forces are internal.

With both objects in the system, the Earth's pull on the ball and the ball's pull on the Earth are a third-law pair of internal forces. Their impulses are equal and opposite, so the ball gains downward momentum exactly as fast as the Earth gains upward momentum, and the total stays constant.

A student who thinks the Earth is too massive to be affected picks this. The ball pulls up on the Earth, so the Earth's momentum changes by as much as the ball's, in the opposite direction; its change in velocity is just far too small to notice.
questions.explain: With both objects in the system, the Earth's pull on the ball and the ball's pull on the Earth are a third-law pair of internal forces. Their impulses are equal and opposite, so the ball gains downward momentum exactly as fast as the Earth gains upward momentum, and the total stays constant.

questions.q: A box slides across a level floor and comes to rest because of friction. Which statement about the box's momentum is correct?
options: It was transferred to the Earth by friction, so the box–Earth total did not change.
It was destroyed by friction, which turned it into thermal energy in the box and floor.
It was not conserved, since momentum is conserved only in collisions and explosions.
It was transferred to the Earth, which gained the speed that the box lost.
optionWhy: Friction from the floor gave the box a backward impulse, and the box gave the floor, and the Earth it is attached to, an equal and opposite forward impulse. The momentum the box lost was transferred to the Earth, so the momentum of the box–Earth system is unchanged.
A student who thinks momentum can be dissipated like kinetic energy picks this. Friction transforms the box's kinetic energy into thermal energy, but momentum is only transferred: here, to the Earth.
A student who links conservation of momentum only to collisions picks this. Momentum is conserved in all interactions, including friction: the box's loss is the Earth's gain.

A student who gives interacting objects equal and opposite changes in velocity picks this. The interaction gives the box and the Earth equal and opposite changes in momentum, not in velocity; with its enormous mass, the Earth's change in velocity is immeasurably small.
questions.explain: Friction from the floor gave the box a backward impulse, and the box gave the floor, and the Earth it is attached to, an equal and opposite forward impulse. The momentum the box lost was transferred to the Earth, so the momentum of the box–Earth system is unchanged.

questions.q: The diagram shows three carts moving along a straight, level track. What is the speed of the center of mass of the three-cart system?
optionWhy: A student who adds the momentum magnitudes picks this: (6.0 + 6.0 + 20)/8.0 = 4.0 m/s. The 3.0 kg cart moves left, so its momentum, −6.0 kg·m/s, cancels part of the others'.
A student who averages the three velocities without weighting them by mass picks this: (6.0 − 2.0 + 5.0)/3 = 3.0 m/s. The carts' masses differ, so each velocity must be weighted by its mass.
Take right as positive and add the momenta with their signs: (1.0)(6.0) + (3.0)(−2.0) + (4.0)(5.0) = 20 kg·m/s. Dividing by the total mass, 8.0 kg, gives v_cm = 2.5 m/s, to the right.
A student who gives the system the velocity of its most massive cart, the 4.0 kg cart, picks this. The other carts contribute too: with every momentum included, v_cm = 20/8.0 = 2.5 m/s.
questions.explain: Take right as positive and add the momenta with their signs: (1.0)(6.0) + (3.0)(−2.0) + (4.0)(5.0) = 20 kg·m/s. Dividing by the total mass, 8.0 kg, gives v_cm = 2.5 m/s, to the right.
questions.working: Right positive. Σp = (1.0 kg)(+6.0 m/s) + (3.0 kg)(−2.0 m/s) + (4.0 kg)(+5.0 m/s) = 6.0 − 6.0 + 20 = +20 kg·m/s. Σm = 8.0 kg. v_cm = (20 kg·m/s)/(8.0 kg) = +2.5 m/s, so the speed is 2.5 m/s (to the right).

questions.q: A ball moving at speed v collides head-on with a ball of greater mass that is at rest on a frictionless surface. The collision is elastic. Which statement about the collision is correct?
options: The moving ball loses kinetic energy; the struck ball gains the same amount.
Each ball has the same kinetic energy after the collision as it had before.
The balls exchange velocities, so the struck ball moves off with speed v.
The moving ball bounces back at speed v, while the struck ball stays at rest.
optionWhy: In an elastic collision the system's total kinetic energy is unchanged, but the balls' individual kinetic energies change: the struck ball starts moving, so it gains kinetic energy, and the moving ball loses exactly that amount.

A student who applies 'kinetic energy is conserved' to each ball separately picks this. Only the total is conserved; the struck ball gains kinetic energy, so the moving ball must lose the same amount.

A student who generalizes Newton's cradle picks this. Velocities are exchanged only for equal masses; with a heavier struck ball, the moving ball rebounds and the struck ball moves off more slowly than v.
A student who treats the heavier ball as a fixed wall picks this. The struck ball is free to move, so it gains momentum and kinetic energy, and the moving ball rebounds more slowly than v.
questions.explain: In an elastic collision the system's total kinetic energy is unchanged, but the balls' individual kinetic energies change: the struck ball starts moving, so it gains kinetic energy, and the moving ball loses exactly that amount.

questions.q: Two carts with clay bumpers collide and stick together on a level track with negligible friction. Just after the collision, the carts' total kinetic energy is less than it was before. Which statement best accounts for the decrease?
options: Nonconservative forces in the clay destroyed some of it, so the total energy decreased.
Nonconservative forces in the clay turned some of it into internal energy and sound.
Nonconservative forces in the clay removed some of it along with part of the momentum.
Nonconservative forces in the clay remove exactly half of it whenever two objects stick.
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy can be destroyed picks this. The missing kinetic energy has been transformed into other forms, mainly internal energy; the total energy is unchanged.

As the clay deforms permanently, nonconservative forces do work that transforms part of the kinetic energy into internal (thermal) energy of the clay and carts, and into sound. The total energy is conserved; that kinetic energy is not restored.

A student who thinks momentum is lost along with kinetic energy picks this. With negligible external impulse, the carts' total momentum is the same before and after; only kinetic energy is transformed.

A student who generalizes the identical-cart example picks this. The fraction transformed depends on the masses: for a cart striking another at rest, it is m₂/(m₁ + m₂), one half only when the masses are equal.
questions.explain: As the clay deforms permanently, nonconservative forces do work that transforms part of the kinetic energy into internal (thermal) energy of the clay and carts, and into sound. The total energy is conserved; that kinetic energy is not restored.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a 1.0 kg cart at rest on a level track with negligible friction. Immediately after the collision, the 2.0 kg cart moves at 1.2 m/s and the 1.0 kg cart moves at 3.6 m/s, both in the original direction of motion. How much of the system's kinetic energy is transformed into other forms in the collision?
optionWhy: A student who thinks kinetic energy is conserved whenever momentum is picks this. Momentum is conserved here (6.0 kg·m/s before and after), but the total kinetic energy falls from 9.0 J to 7.92 J.
Before: K = ½(2.0)(3.0)² = 9.0 J. After: K = ½(2.0)(1.2)² + ½(1.0)(3.6)² = 1.44 + 6.48 = 7.92 J. The decrease, 9.0 − 7.92 ≈ 1.1 J, is transformed by nonconservative forces into other forms.
A student who writes kinetic energy as mv² picks this: 18 J − (2.88 J + 12.96 J) ≈ 2.2 J. With K = ½mv², the totals are 9.0 J and 7.92 J, a decrease of 1.1 J.
A student who counts all the kinetic energy lost by the 2.0 kg cart as transformed picks this: 9.0 − ½(2.0)(1.2)² ≈ 7.6 J. Most of that energy, 6.48 J, became kinetic energy of the 1.0 kg cart.
questions.explain: Before: K = ½(2.0)(3.0)² = 9.0 J. After: K = ½(2.0)(1.2)² + ½(1.0)(3.6)² = 1.44 + 6.48 = 7.92 J. The decrease, 9.0 − 7.92 ≈ 1.1 J, is transformed by nonconservative forces into other forms.

questions.q: Cart A collides with an identical cart B, which is at rest on a level track with negligible friction. Three trials, I, II and III, are run with the same initial velocity of A. The diagram shows the carts' velocities before the collision and just after it in each trial. Which ranks the kinetic energy transformed into other forms in the three trials?
options: I > III > II
I > II = III
I = II = III
II > III > I
optionWhy: With each cart of mass m, the kinetic energy before is ½m(4.0)² = 8.0m (in J, with m in kg). After: I, ½(2m)(2.0)² = 4.0m; II, ½m(4.0)² = 8.0m; III, ½m(1.0)² + ½m(3.0)² = 5.0m. Energy transformed: I, 4.0m; II, 0; III, 3.0m.
A student who thinks only collisions in which the carts stick are inelastic picks this. In III the carts separate, but their total kinetic energy falls from 8.0m to 5.0m, so 3.0m is transformed.

A student who takes kinetic energy to be proportional to speed finds the same total, proportional to 4.0 m/s, in every trial, and picks this. Kinetic energy depends on v², so 1.0² + 3.0² = 10 is less than 4.0² = 16, and 2 × 2.0² = 8 is less again.
A student who counts the kinetic energy lost by A as transformed picks this: A loses all its kinetic energy in II. In II that energy all goes to B as kinetic energy, so none is transformed.
questions.explain: With each cart of mass m, the kinetic energy before is ½m(4.0)² = 8.0m (in J, with m in kg). After: I, ½(2m)(2.0)² = 4.0m; II, ½m(4.0)² = 8.0m; III, ½m(1.0)² + ½m(3.0)² = 5.0m. Energy transformed: I, 4.0m; II, 0; III, 3.0m.
questions.working: K₀ = ½m(4.0)² = 8.0m. After: I = ½(2m)(2.0)² = 4.0m; II = ½m(4.0)² = 8.0m; III = ½m(1.0)² + ½m(3.0)² = 5.0m. Transformed: I 4.0m, II 0, III 3.0m → I > III > II. (Momentum is 4.0m in every trial.)

questions.q: Cart X, of mass m, moving at speed v₀ along a level track with negligible friction, collides with and sticks to cart Y, which is at rest. In trial 1, Y has mass m. In trial 2, Y has mass 2m, and X has the same initial speed. What is the ratio of the kinetic energy transformed into other forms in trial 2 to that in trial 1?
optionWhy: A student who counts the kinetic energy lost by X as transformed picks this: X loses K₀(1 − 1/4) in trial 1 and K₀(1 − 1/9) in trial 2, a ratio of 32/27 ≈ 1.19. Part of what X loses becomes Y's kinetic energy, which is not transformed.
A student who thinks exactly half the kinetic energy is transformed whenever objects stick picks this. That is true only for equal masses; with Y of mass 2m, two thirds is transformed.

Initial kinetic energy K₀ = ½mv₀² in both trials. Trial 1: v = v₀/2, K after = ½(2m)(v₀/2)² = K₀/2, so K₀/2 is transformed. Trial 2: v = v₀/3, K after = ½(3m)(v₀/3)² = K₀/3, so 2K₀/3 is transformed. The ratio is (2/3)/(1/2) = 1.33.

A student who takes the common velocity to be the plain average, v₀/2, in both trials picks this: K₀/2 is transformed in trial 1 but only K₀/4 in trial 2. The common velocity is the mass-weighted average, v₀/3 in trial 2.
questions.explain: Initial kinetic energy K₀ = ½mv₀² in both trials. Trial 1: v = v₀/2, K after = ½(2m)(v₀/2)² = K₀/2, so K₀/2 is transformed. Trial 2: v = v₀/3, K after = ½(3m)(v₀/3)² = K₀/3, so 2K₀/3 is transformed. The ratio is (2/3)/(1/2) = 1.33.
questions.working: K₀ = ½mv₀². Trial 1: v = mv₀/(2m) = v₀/2; K_f = ½(2m)(v₀²/4) = K₀/2; transformed K₀/2. Trial 2: v = v₀/3; K_f = ½(3m)(v₀²/9) = K₀/3; transformed 2K₀/3. Ratio = (2/3)/(1/2) = 4/3 ≈ 1.33. (Checked with sympy.)
